title: Extractor Functions
text:
extract_arguments
Retrieve the arguments used when fitting a model with bgm() or bgmCompare().
extract_arguments(bgms_object)



Argument
Description




bgms_object
A fitted bgms or bgmCompare object.



Returns a named list containing all arguments passed to the fitting function, including data dimensions, prior settings, and MCMC configuration.

title: Extractor Functions
text:
extract_main_effects
Retrieve posterior mean main-effect parameters.
extract_main_effects(bgms_object)



Argument
Description




bgms_object
A fitted bgms or bgmCompare object.



The structure depends on the model type:

GGM (bgms): NULL. GGM models have no main effects; the precision matrix diagonal is on coef(fit)$pairwise.
OMRF (bgms): A numeric matrix (p x max_categories) of posterior mean category thresholds. Columns beyond the number of categories for a variable are NA.
Mixed MRF (bgms): A list with $discrete (threshold matrix) and $continuous (means matrix).
bgmCompare: A matrix with one row per post-warmup iteration, containing posterior samples of baseline main-effect parameters.

title: Extractor Functions
text:
extract_pairwise_interactions
Retrieve posterior samples of pairwise interaction parameters.
extract_pairwise_interactions(bgms_object)



Argument
Description




bgms_object
A fitted bgms or bgmCompare object.



Returns a matrix with one row per post-warmup iteration and one column per edge. For bgmCompare, columns correspond to baseline pairwise interaction parameters.

title: Extractor Functions
text:
extract_indicators
Retrieve posterior samples of inclusion indicators.
extract_indicators(bgms_object)



Argument
Description




bgms_object
A fitted bgms or bgmCompare object.



Returns a matrix with one row per post-warmup iteration and one column per indicator, containing binary (0/1) samples:

bgms: One column per edge. Requires edge_selection = TRUE.
bgmCompare: Columns for main-effect and pairwise difference indicators. Requires difference_selection = TRUE.

title: Extractor Functions
text:
extract_posterior_inclusion_probabilities
Compute posterior inclusion probabilities.
extract_posterior_inclusion_probabilities(bgms_object)



Argument
Description




bgms_object
A fitted bgms or bgmCompare object.



Returns a symmetric p x p matrix of posterior inclusion probabilities:

bgms: Off-diagonal entries are edge inclusion probabilities. Requires edge_selection = TRUE.
bgmCompare: Diagonal entries are main-effect inclusion probabilities; off-diagonal entries are pairwise difference inclusion probabilities. Requires difference_selection = TRUE.

title: Extractor Functions
text:
extract_indicator_priors
Retrieve the prior specification used for inclusion indicators.
extract_indicator_priors(bgms_object)



Argument
Description




bgms_object
A fitted bgms or bgmCompare object.



Returns a named list describing the prior structure, including the prior type and hyperparameters:

bgms: Requires edge_selection = TRUE. Returns the prior type ("Bernoulli", "Beta-Bernoulli", or "Stochastic-Block") and associated hyperparameters.
bgmCompare: Requires difference_selection = TRUE. Returns the difference prior specification.

title: Extractor Functions
text:
extract_group_params
Compute group-specific parameter estimates by combining baseline parameters and group differences.
extract_group_params(bgms_object)



Argument
Description




bgms_object
A fitted bgmCompare object.



Returns a list with main_effects_groups (main effects per group) and pairwise_effects_groups (pairwise effects per group).

title: Extractor Functions
text:
extract_sbm
Retrieve posterior summaries from a model fitted with the Stochastic Block prior.
extract_sbm(bgms_object)



Argument
Description




bgms_object
A fitted bgms object.



Requires edge_selection = TRUE and edge_prior = "Stochastic-Block". Returns a list with:

posterior_num_blocks — Posterior probabilities for each possible number of clusters.
posterior_mean_allocations — Posterior mean cluster allocations.
posterior_mode_allocations — Posterior mode cluster allocations.
posterior_mean_coclustering_matrix — Co-clustering proportion matrix.

title: Extractor Functions
text:
extract_ess
Retrieve effective sample size estimates for all parameters.
extract_ess(bgms_object)



Argument
Description




bgms_object
A fitted bgms or bgmCompare object.



Returns a named list with ESS values for each parameter type present in the model (e.g., main, pairwise, indicator).

title: Extractor Functions
text:
extract_rhat
Retrieve R-hat convergence diagnostics for all parameters.
extract_rhat(bgms_object)



Argument
Description




bgms_object
A fitted bgms or bgmCompare object.



Returns a named list with R-hat values for each parameter type present in the model (e.g., main, pairwise, indicator).

title: S3 Methods
text:
coef
Extract posterior mean coefficients.

bgms
coef(object, ...)



Argument
Description




object
An object of class bgms.


...
Ignored.



Returns a list with:

main — Posterior mean main-effect parameters. NULL for GGM models. For OMRF models: a numeric matrix (p x max_categories) of category thresholds. For mixed MRF models: a list with $discrete (threshold matrix) and $continuous (means matrix).
pairwise — Posterior mean pairwise interaction matrix. For GGM and mixed MRF models the precision matrix diagonal is included on the diagonal.
indicator — Posterior mean edge inclusion indicators (if available).



bgmCompare
coef(object, ...)



Argument
Description




object
An object of class bgmCompare.


...
Ignored.



Returns a list with:

main_effects_raw — Posterior means of raw main-effect parameters (variables x (baseline + differences)).
pairwise_effects_raw — Posterior means of raw pairwise-effect parameters (pairs x (baseline + differences)).
main_effects_groups — Posterior means of group-specific main effects (variables x groups), computed as baseline plus projected differences.
pairwise_effects_groups — Posterior means of group-specific pairwise effects (pairs x groups), computed as baseline plus projected differences.
indicators — Posterior mean inclusion probabilities as a symmetric matrix, with diagonals for main effects and off-diagonals for pairwise effects.

title: S3 Methods
text:
predict
Compute conditional probability distributions for one or more variables given the observed values of other variables in the data.

bgms
predict(object, newdata, variables = NULL,
        type = c("probabilities", "response"),
        method = c("posterior-mean", "posterior-sample"),
        ndraws = NULL, seed = NULL, ...)







Argument
Description




object
An object of class bgms.


newdata
A matrix or data frame with n rows and p columns. Must match the variables used in fitting.


variables
Character vector of names, integer vector of column indices, or NULL (all variables).


type
"probabilities" (full conditional distribution) or "response" (predicted category).


method
"posterior-mean" (use posterior means) or "posterior-sample" (average over draws).


ndraws
Number of posterior draws for "posterior-sample". NULL uses all draws.


seed
Optional random seed.



Ordinal models: For type = "probabilities", returns a named list with one matrix per variable (n rows x (num_categories + 1) columns). For type = "response", returns a matrix of predicted categories.
GGM models: For type = "probabilities", returns a list with one matrix per variable (n rows x 2 columns: "mean" and "sd"). For type = "response", returns conditional means.
Mixed MRF models: Returns a list combining both formats for discrete and continuous variables.
When method = "posterior-sample", predictions include an "sd" attribute with the standard deviation across draws.


bgmCompare
predict(object, newdata, group, variables = NULL,
        type = c("probabilities", "response"),
        method = c("posterior-mean"), ...)







Argument
Description




object
An object of class bgmCompare.


newdata
A matrix or data frame matching the original variables.


group
Integer specifying which group’s parameters to use (1 to number of groups). Required.


variables
Which variables to predict (character, integer, or NULL for all).


type
"probabilities" or "response".


method
"posterior-mean" (posterior mean parameters).



Returns the same structure as predict.bgms, using group-specific parameters obtained by combining baseline parameters and group differences.

title: S3 Methods
text:
simulate
Generate new observations from a fitted model.

bgms
simulate(object, nsim = 500, seed = NULL,
         method = c("posterior-mean", "posterior-sample"),
         ndraws = NULL, iter = 1000,
         cores = parallel::detectCores(),
         display_progress = c("per-chain", "total", "none"), ...)







Argument
Description




object
An object of class bgms.


nsim
Number of observations to simulate. Default: 500.


seed
Optional random seed.


method
"posterior-mean" (single simulation) or "posterior-sample" (one dataset per draw, parallel).


ndraws
Number of posterior draws for "posterior-sample". NULL uses all.


iter
Gibbs iterations for equilibration. Default: 1000.


cores
CPU cores for parallel execution with "posterior-sample".


display_progress
Progress bar style: "per-chain", "total", or "none".



If method = "posterior-mean": a matrix (nsim x p). If method = "posterior-sample": a list of matrices, one per posterior draw. For mixed MRF models, discrete columns contain integers and continuous columns contain real values.


bgmCompare
simulate(object, nsim = 500, seed = NULL, group,
         method = c("posterior-mean"), iter = 1000, ...)







Argument
Description




object
An object of class bgmCompare.


nsim
Number of observations to simulate. Default: 500.


seed
Optional random seed.


group
Integer specifying which group to simulate from (1 to number of groups). Required.


method
"posterior-mean".


iter
Gibbs iterations for equilibration. Default: 1000.



Returns a matrix (nsim x p) of simulated observations for the specified group.

title: S3 Methods
text:
simulate_mrf
Simulate observations from a Markov Random Field using user-specified parameters (no fitted model needed).
simulate_mrf(
  num_states,
  num_variables,
  num_categories,
  pairwise,
  main,
  variable_type = "ordinal",
  baseline_category,
  iter = 1000,
  seed = NULL
)







Argument
Description




num_states
Number of observations to generate.


num_variables
Number of variables in the MRF.


num_categories
Integer or integer vector. Number of response categories on top of the base category (1 = binary).


pairwise
Symmetric matrix of pairwise interactions. For continuous variables, this is the precision matrix (must be positive definite).


main
Main-effect parameters. For ordinal variables: a matrix of category thresholds. For continuous variables: a means vector.


variable_type
"ordinal", "blume-capel", or "continuous". Can be a vector for mixed types (ordinal/Blume-Capel only).


baseline_category
Integer vector of baseline categories for Blume–Capel variables.


iter
Gibbs iterations for equilibration (ordinal only). Default: 1000.


seed
Optional random seed.



Returns a (num_states x num_variables) matrix of simulated observations.
For ordinal and Blume-Capel variables, the Gibbs sampler generates observations from full conditional distributions. For continuous variables, observations are drawn directly from \(N(\mu, \Omega^{-1})\).

title: Edge Selection
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
Bayesian edge selection determines which edges are present in the network by placing spike-and-slab priors on the pairwise interaction parameters. When edge_selection = TRUE (the default), bgm() estimates both the edge structure and the effect sizes simultaneously.

title: Edge Selection
text:
Spike-and-slab priors
For each edge \((i, j)\), an indicator variable \(\gamma_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}\) governs whether the interaction is included in the model:

When \(\gamma_{ij} = 0\) (spike), the interaction \(\sigma_{ij}\) is set to exactly zero — the edge is absent.
When \(\gamma_{ij} = 1\) (slab), the interaction receives a Cauchy prior with scale pairwise_scale — the edge is present and the effect size is estimated.

The prior probability of inclusion is controlled by the edge_prior argument. See Prior Basics for the available options (Bernoulli, Beta-Bernoulli, Stochastic-Block).

title: Edge Selection
text:
Posterior inclusion probabilities
The posterior inclusion probability for edge \((i, j)\) is the posterior mean of \(\gamma_{ij}\): the proportion of MCMC iterations in which the edge was included. It ranges from 0 to 1:

Values near 1.0: strong evidence that the edge is present
Values near 0.0: strong evidence that the edge is absent
Values near 0.5: inconclusive (neither inclusion nor exclusion is strongly supported)

These are reported by coef(fit)$indicator and in the summary() output.

title: Edge Selection
text:
Bayes factors for edges
When the prior inclusion probability is 0.5, the posterior inclusion probability can be directly transformed into a Bayes factor:
\[
\text{BF}_{10} = \frac{p(\gamma_{ij} = 1 \mid \mathbf{x})}{1 - p(\gamma_{ij} = 1 \mid \mathbf{x})}
\]
For other prior inclusion probabilities, the Bayes factor accounts for the prior odds:
\[
\text{BF}_{10} = \frac{p(\gamma_{ij} = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}) / p(\gamma_{ij} = 0 \mid \mathbf{x})}{p(\gamma_{ij} = 1) / p(\gamma_{ij} = 0)}
\]
The reciprocal \(1 / \text{BF}_{10}\) quantifies the evidence for edge absence.

title: Edge Selection
text:
Evidence categories
The following classification, based on Kass and Raftery (1995), is a common convention:



Bayes factor
Evidence




1–3
Weak


3–10
Moderate


10–100
Strong


> 100
Decisive



The same scale applies for evidence of absence using \(1 / \text{BF}_{10}\).

title: Edge Selection
text:
Median probability model
A common summary of the posterior network is the median probability model: retain all edges with posterior inclusion probability above 0.5. This corresponds to including edges for which there is more evidence for presence than absence.
network = coef(fit)$pairwise
network[coef(fit)$indicator < 0.5] = 0

title: Edge Selection
text:
Prior guidance for edge selection
The default inclusion_probability = 0.5 with a Bernoulli prior is a standard noninformative choice. Considerations for changing it:

Sparse networks: lower the inclusion probability (e.g., 0.25) to encode a prior expectation that most edges are absent.
Dense networks: raise the inclusion probability if prior knowledge suggests many edges.
Learned inclusion probability: use edge_prior = "Beta-Bernoulli" to let the data inform the overall sparsity level.
Structured sparsity: use edge_prior = "Stochastic-Block" when edges are expected to cluster (see Edge Clustering).

The pairwise_scale parameter controls the slab width. A wider slab makes it harder for the Bayes factor to favor inclusion when the true effect is small, because the prior spreads probability over a wide range. The default of 2.5 balances sensitivity to small effects against specificity.

title: The Bayesian Approach
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
bgms uses Bayesian inference to estimate graphical models. This means that all unknown quantities — interaction parameters, edge inclusion indicators, and model structure — are treated as random variables with probability distributions. The output is a posterior distribution, not a single point estimate.

title: The Bayesian Approach
text:
Prior, likelihood, posterior
Bayesian inference combines a prior distribution with the likelihood of the observed data to produce a posterior distribution. For a parameter \(\theta\) and data \(\mathbf{x}\):
\[
p(\theta \mid \mathbf{x}) \propto p(\mathbf{x} \mid \theta) \; p(\theta)
\]

The prior \(p(\theta)\) encodes assumptions about the parameter before observing data. In bgms, priors are placed on interaction parameters, main effects, and edge indicators. See Prior Basics for details.
The likelihood \(p(\mathbf{x} \mid \theta)\) measures how well the model with parameter value \(\theta\) explains the observed data.
The posterior \(p(\theta \mid \mathbf{x})\) is the updated distribution of \(\theta\) after observing the data. All inference — point estimates, intervals, hypothesis tests — comes from this posterior.

title: The Bayesian Approach
text:
Posterior summaries
bgms summarizes the posterior with several quantities:

Posterior mean: the average of the posterior distribution. Reported by coef() and in the summary() output.
Posterior standard deviation: the spread of the posterior. A small standard deviation indicates a precise estimate.
Credible intervals: ranges that contain the parameter with a given posterior probability (e.g., a 95% credible interval). Unlike frequentist confidence intervals, credible intervals have a direct probability interpretation.

title: The Bayesian Approach
text:
Bayes factors
For edge selection, bgms uses Bayes factors to quantify evidence for the presence or absence of each edge. The inclusion Bayes factor for edge \((i, j)\) is:
\[
\text{BF}_{10} = \frac{p(\gamma_{ij} = 1 \mid \mathbf{x})}{p(\gamma_{ij} = 0 \mid \mathbf{x})} \bigg/ \frac{p(\gamma_{ij} = 1)}{p(\gamma_{ij} = 0)}
\]
where \(\gamma_{ij}\) is the binary indicator for edge inclusion. When the prior inclusion probability is 0.5, this simplifies to the posterior odds:
\[
\text{BF}_{10} = \frac{p(\gamma_{ij} = 1 \mid \mathbf{x})}{1 - p(\gamma_{ij} = 1 \mid \mathbf{x})}
\]
A Bayes factor greater than 1 favors edge inclusion; less than 1 favors exclusion. The reciprocal \(1 / \text{BF}_{10}\) gives the evidence for exclusion. See Edge Selection for interpretation guidelines.

title: The Bayesian Approach
text:
How bgms uses MCMC
The posterior distributions in bgms do not have closed-form solutions. Instead, bgms draws samples from the posterior using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. The default sampler is the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS), an adaptive form of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. bgms also supports fixed-length HMC and adaptive Metropolis-Hastings.
Multiple chains run in parallel to diagnose convergence. Key diagnostics — effective sample size (ESS), R-hat, and energy diagnostics — are described in MCMC Diagnostics. The structure of the raw MCMC output is described in MCMC Output.

title: Gaussian Graphical Model
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
The Gaussian graphical model (GGM) is a Markov Random Field for continuous variables. In bgms, the GGM is fit when variable_type = "continuous".

title: Gaussian Graphical Model
text:
The model
A GGM assumes that \(p\) continuous variables follow a multivariate normal distribution:
\[
\mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})
\]
The network structure is encoded in the precision matrix \(\boldsymbol{K} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\). A zero entry \(K_{ij} = 0\) means that variables \(i\) and \(j\) are conditionally independent given all other variables — equivalently, the edge between nodes \(i\) and \(j\) is absent.

title: Gaussian Graphical Model
text:
Partial correlations
The off-diagonal entries of the standardized precision matrix are partial correlations:
\[
\rho_{ij \cdot \text{rest}} = -\frac{K_{ij}}{\sqrt{K_{ii} K_{jj}}}
\]
A positive partial correlation means that, holding all other variables constant, higher values of \(x_i\) are associated with higher values of \(x_j\). bgms reports these partial correlations as the pairwise interaction parameters.

title: Gaussian Graphical Model
text:
Fitting a GGM
To fit a GGM, pass continuous data and set variable_type:
fit = bgm(x = continuous_data, variable_type = "continuous", seed = 1234)
The summary() and coef() methods work the same as for ordinal models. The pairwise effects in the output are partial correlations, and the diagonal of the pairwise matrix contains the precision matrix diagonal.

title: Gaussian Graphical Model
text:
Edge selection
When edge_selection = TRUE (the default), bgms applies spike-and-slab priors to the off-diagonal entries of the precision matrix. Edges with posterior inclusion probability above 0.5 have more evidence for presence than absence. See Edge Selection for details.

title: Gaussian Graphical Model
text:
Missing data
For continuous data, missing values can be imputed within the MCMC sampler by setting na_action = "impute". Missing entries are resampled at each iteration from their full conditional distribution. The default behavior is na_action = "listwise", which removes rows with any missing values before fitting.

title: Group Comparison
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
The bgmCompare() function tests for differences in network structure between groups. It estimates whether pairwise interactions and category thresholds differ across groups in an ordinal Markov Random Field.

title: Group Comparison
text:
The model
For each pair of variables \((i, j)\), the group-specific interaction is decomposed as:
\[
\theta_{ij}^{(g)} = \phi_{ij} + \delta_{ij}^{(g)}
\]
where \(\phi_{ij}\) is the baseline effect (shared across groups) and \(\delta_{ij}^{(g)}\) is the group-specific difference, constrained so that the differences sum to zero across groups. The same decomposition applies to category threshold parameters.

title: Group Comparison
text:
Defining groups
Groups can be specified in two ways:
Two separate datasets — pass x (Group 1) and y (Group 2):
fit = bgmCompare(x = data_group1, y = data_group2, seed = 1234)
Group membership vector — pass a single dataset with a group indicator:
fit = bgmCompare(x = data, group_indicator = groups, seed = 1234)
The group_indicator approach supports more than two groups.

title: Group Comparison
text:
Difference selection
When difference_selection = TRUE (the default), spike-and-slab priors are placed on the difference parameters \(\delta_{ij}^{(g)}\). The posterior inclusion probability for each difference indicates how plausible it is that the groups differ on that parameter.
By default, only pairwise interaction differences are selected (main_difference_selection = FALSE). Main effect (threshold) differences are always included. This default reflects that main effects are often nuisance parameters, and their selection can interfere with pairwise selection under the Beta-Bernoulli prior.

title: Group Comparison
text:
Interpreting the output
The summary() method reports:

Baseline effects: posterior summaries for the shared parameters \(\phi_{ij}\).
Difference effects: posterior summaries for the group differences \(\delta_{ij}^{(g)}\), including inclusion probabilities and Bayes factors.

The coef() method returns:

$pairwise_effects_groups: group-specific posterior mean pairwise interactions (baseline + difference).
$main_effects_groups: group-specific posterior mean thresholds.
$indicator: posterior inclusion probabilities for differences.

title: Group Comparison
text:
Bayes factors for group differences
When difference_probability = 0.5 (the default), the Bayes factor for a group difference equals the posterior odds:
\[
\text{BF}_{10} = \frac{p(\gamma = 1 \mid \mathbf{x})}{1 - p(\gamma = 1 \mid \mathbf{x})}
\]
A large Bayes factor indicates that the groups differ on that parameter; a small one (or equivalently, a large \(1 / \text{BF}_{10}\)) indicates that they do not.

title: Group Comparison
text:
Prior guidance for group comparison

difference_scale = 1 (default): scale of the Cauchy prior for difference parameters. This is smaller than the default pairwise_scale (2.5) because group differences are typically smaller than the effects themselves.
difference_prior = "Bernoulli" (default): fixed inclusion probability for differences. "Beta-Bernoulli" lets the data inform the overall rate of group differences.
difference_probability = 0.5 (default): prior probability that any given difference is nonzero.

title: Group Comparison
text:
References
Marsman, M., Waldorp, L. J., Sekulovski, N., & Haslbeck, J. M. B. (2025). Bayes factor tests for group differences in ordinal and binary graphical models. Psychometrika, 90(5), 1809–1842.

title: Graphical Models
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
A graphical model represents the statistical relationships among a set of variables as a graph. Each variable is a node, and edges between nodes encode direct statistical associations. bgms estimates undirected graphical models — specifically, Markov Random Fields.

title: Graphical Models
text:
Nodes and edges
In a graphical model, the \(p\) variables in a dataset are represented as nodes (or vertices) of a graph. An edge between two nodes indicates a direct statistical association between the corresponding variables, after accounting for all other variables in the model.
The absence of an edge between two nodes means that the two variables are conditionally independent given the remaining variables. This is the key interpretive property of undirected graphical models: the graph encodes the conditional independence structure of the joint distribution.

title: Graphical Models
text:
Conditional independence
Two variables \(X_i\) and \(X_j\) are conditionally independent given the rest if knowing the value of \(X_i\) provides no additional information about \(X_j\) once all other variables are observed. In the graph, this corresponds to the absence of a direct edge between nodes \(i\) and \(j\).
Conditional independence is distinct from marginal independence. Two variables may be marginally correlated (both associated with a third variable) yet conditionally independent once that third variable is accounted for. The graphical model separates direct from indirect associations.

title: Graphical Models
text:
Markov Random Fields
A Markov Random Field (MRF) is an undirected graphical model in which the joint distribution of the variables factorizes according to the graph structure. For a set of \(p\) variables with observations \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_p)\), the MRF specifies:
\[
p(\mathbf{x}) \propto \exp\left(\sum_{i} \theta_i(x_i) +
\sum_{i < j} \sigma_{ij} \, s_i(x_i) \, s_j(x_j)\right)
\]
where \(\theta_i(x_i)\) are main effects (node potentials), \(\sigma_{ij}\) are pairwise interaction parameters, and \(s_i(x_i)\) are sufficient statistics that depend on the variable type.
The pairwise interaction \(\sigma_{ij}\) controls the edge between nodes \(i\) and \(j\): when \(\sigma_{ij} = 0\), the edge is absent and the two variables are conditionally independent.

title: Graphical Models
text:
Model families in bgms
bgms supports three model families, all MRFs:

Ordinal MRF — for binary and ordinal variables. Category thresholds serve as main effects, and pairwise interactions capture associations between ordinal scores. See Ordinal MRF.
Gaussian Graphical Model (GGM) — for continuous variables. The precision matrix (inverse covariance matrix) determines the edge structure: nonzero off-diagonal entries correspond to edges. See GGM.
Mixed MRF — for datasets containing both discrete and continuous variables. Combines the ordinal MRF and GGM into a joint model. See Mixed MRF.

title: Graphical Models
text:
Why networks?
In psychology and the social sciences, graphical models are used to study how symptoms, attitudes, or behaviors relate to each other directly, rather than through latent constructs. Estimating the conditional independence structure — the network — identifies which pairs of variables have direct associations and which are only indirectly related.
Bayesian methods add the ability to quantify evidence for the presence or absence of each edge, rather than relying on thresholding rules applied to point estimates. bgms implements this through Bayesian edge selection with spike-and-slab priors (see Edge Selection).

title: Getting Started
text:
Network plot
To visualize the estimated network, threshold inclusion probabilities at 0.5 and plot the result using the qgraph package.

library(qgraph)

median_probability_network = coef(fit)$pairwise
median_probability_network[coef(fit)$indicator < 0.5] = 0.0

qgraph(median_probability_network,
  theme = "TeamFortress",
  maximum = 1,
  fade = FALSE,
  color = c("#f0ae0e"), vsize = 10, repulsion = .9,
  label.cex = 1, label.scale = "FALSE",
  labels = colnames(data)
)

Edges with posterior inclusion probability below 0.5 are set to zero, so only edges with at least moderate evidence of inclusion appear in the plot.

title: Getting Started
text:
Continuous data
For continuous variables, bgm() fits a Gaussian graphical model. Set variable_type = "continuous":
fit_ggm = bgm(continuous_data, variable_type = "continuous", seed = 1234)
summary(fit_ggm)
The pairwise effects are partial correlations (off-diagonal entries of the standardized precision matrix). Missing values can be imputed during sampling with na_action = "impute".

title: User’s Guide
text:
The User’s Guide covers conceptual background and practical tutorials for bgms. It is organized into four parts: background concepts, model types, analysis workflows, and MCMC output.

Background

Getting Started — Installation and first model fit
Graphical Models — Nodes, edges, and conditional independence
The Bayesian Approach — Priors, posteriors, and Bayes factors
Prior Basics — How bgms uses priors and when to change defaults



Models

Gaussian Graphical Model — Continuous data, partial correlations, precision matrix
Ordinal MRF — Binary and ordinal data, category thresholds, pairwise interactions
Mixed MRF — Datasets with both continuous and discrete variables



Analyses

Edge Selection — Spike-and-slab priors for structure learning
Group Comparison — Comparing networks across groups with bgmCompare()
Edge Clustering — Stochastic block model prior for discovering edge clusters



MCMC Output

MCMC Output — What the sampler returns and how to access it
MCMC Diagnostics — Convergence checks: ESS, R-hat, trace plots, divergences



Prerequisites
This guide assumes basic familiarity with R programming and the goals of network analysis. The Background chapters introduce the necessary statistical concepts.

title: Prior Basics
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
This chapter explains what priors are, how bgms uses them, and when the defaults should be changed. Analysis-specific prior guidance appears on the Edge Selection, Group Comparison, and Edge Clustering pages.

title: Prior Basics
text:
What is a prior?
A prior distribution encodes assumptions about a parameter before observing data. In Bayesian inference, the prior is combined with the likelihood to produce the posterior distribution. The prior matters most when data are sparse; as data accumulate, the posterior is increasingly driven by the likelihood.

title: Prior Basics
text:
Priors in bgms
bgms places priors on three types of quantities: pairwise interaction parameters, main effect parameters, and (when edge selection is active) edge inclusion indicators. Each has a distinct role.

Pairwise interaction prior
The pairwise interactions \(\sigma_{ij}\) receive a Cauchy prior (a Student-\(t\) distribution with one degree of freedom) centered at zero. The scale is controlled by pairwise_scale (default: 2.5).
The Cauchy distribution has heavy tails, allowing large effects when supported by the data, while the peak at zero provides moderate shrinkage. In models with many variables and limited data, this regularization prevents extreme estimates.
When standardize = TRUE, the prior scale is adjusted based on the range of response scores. Variables with more categories have larger score products, which typically correspond to smaller interaction effects. Without standardization, a fixed scale is relatively wide for high-category pairs and narrow for low-category pairs. The adjustment ensures equivalent relative shrinkage across all variable pairs.


Main effect prior
Main effects (category threshold parameters for ordinal models) receive a beta-prime prior with shape parameters main_alpha and main_beta (both default to 0.5). When the two shape parameters are equal, the prior is symmetric. The beta-prime distribution is defined on the positive reals and provides light regularization of the threshold parameters.


Edge inclusion prior
When edge_selection = TRUE, each edge has a binary indicator \(\gamma_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}\) governing whether the interaction is included. The prior on these indicators is controlled by edge_prior:



Prior
Parameters
Behavior




"Bernoulli"
inclusion_probability (default 0.5)
Fixed inclusion probability, same for all edges


"Beta-Bernoulli"
beta_bernoulli_alpha, beta_bernoulli_beta (both default 1)
Inclusion probability given a Beta prior, learned from data


"Stochastic-Block"
Multiple (see Clustering)
Cluster-based inclusion probabilities with separate within/between rates

title: Prior Basics
text:
Edge priors vs. parameter priors
These two types of priors serve different purposes:

Edge inclusion priors determine how likely each edge is to be present a priori. They control the sparsity of the estimated network.
Parameter priors (Cauchy for interactions, beta-prime for thresholds) control the regularization of effect sizes. They determine how much shrinkage is applied to nonzero effects.

In a spike-and-slab framework, the “spike” is the prior mass at zero (edge excluded), and the “slab” is the Cauchy prior over effect sizes (edge included). Both matter for the posterior, but they answer different questions: the inclusion prior affects whether an edge is present, while the parameter prior affects how large the estimated effect is.

title: Prior Basics
section: Default choices and when to change them
text:
Default choices and when to change them
The defaults are designed for moderate-sized networks (5–30 variables) with ordinal data and are a reasonable starting point for most analyses:

pairwise_scale = 2.5: Appropriate for standardized ordinal data. Consider increasing it if effects are expected to be large, or decreasing it for stronger shrinkage in dense networks.
inclusion_probability = 0.5: Assigns equal prior weight to edge presence and absence. This is a standard noninformative choice. Lowering it encodes a prior expectation of sparser networks.
main_alpha = 0.5, main_beta = 0.5: A weakly informative symmetric prior. Changing these is rarely necessary unless there is strong prior information about threshold magnitudes.
standardize = FALSE: Turned off by default. Set to TRUE when variables have different numbers of response categories and comparable shrinkage across pairs is desired.

title: Edge Clustering
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
The stochastic block model (SBM) prior in bgms discovers clusters of edges in the network. Nodes are assigned to latent blocks, and edge inclusion probabilities depend on whether the two endpoints belong to the same block or different blocks.

title: Edge Clustering
text:
What is edge clustering?
In many applied networks, edges are not exchangeable: some groups of variables are densely connected while connections between groups are sparse. The SBM prior captures this structure by learning block assignments from the data. Nodes within the same block share a within-cluster inclusion probability, and edges between blocks share a (typically lower) between-cluster inclusion probability.

title: Edge Clustering
text:
Setting up the SBM prior
To use the SBM prior, set edge_prior = "Stochastic-Block" in bgm():
fit = bgm(
  x = data,
  edge_prior = "Stochastic-Block",
  seed = 1234
)
The SBM prior has several hyperparameters:








Parameter
Default
Role




beta_bernoulli_alpha, beta_bernoulli_beta
1, 1
Shape parameters of the Beta prior on within-cluster inclusion probability


beta_bernoulli_alpha_between, beta_bernoulli_beta_between
1, 1
Shape parameters of the Beta prior on between-cluster inclusion probability


dirichlet_alpha
1
Concentration of the Dirichlet prior on block assignments


lambda
1
Rate of the zero-truncated Poisson prior on the number of clusters



With the defaults, the prior is symmetric (within and between clusters have the same Beta(1, 1) prior on inclusion probability) and the number of clusters is determined by the data.

title: Edge Clustering
text:
Interpreting block structure
The extract_sbm() function retrieves the SBM results:
sbm = extract_sbm(fit)
This returns:

posterior_mean_allocations: the estimated cluster assignment for each node, computed using the method of Dahl (2006).
posterior_mode_allocations: the most frequent cluster assignment across iterations.
posterior_coclustering_matrix: a symmetric matrix where entry \((i, j)\) is the proportion of iterations in which nodes \(i\) and \(j\) were assigned to the same cluster. Plotting this matrix reveals the block structure.
posterior_num_blocks: a table of posterior probabilities for each possible number of clusters.

title: Edge Clustering
text:
Prior choices for clustering

lambda controls the expected number of clusters. A small lambda favors fewer clusters; a larger lambda allows more. The zero-truncated Poisson prior ensures at least one cluster.
dirichlet_alpha controls how evenly nodes are distributed across clusters. A value of 1 gives a uniform prior over partitions. Smaller values favor uneven cluster sizes (a few large clusters and several small ones).
The within-cluster Beta parameters control how dense within-cluster connectivity is a priori. Setting beta_bernoulli_alpha > beta_bernoulli_beta favors dense within-cluster connections.
The between-cluster Beta parameters control between-cluster connectivity. Setting beta_bernoulli_beta_between > beta_bernoulli_alpha_between favors sparse between-cluster connections.

title: Edge Clustering
text:
References
Sekulovski, N., Keetelaar, S., Haslbeck, J. M. B., & Marsman, M. (2025). Bayesian variable selection in multilevel and multi-group graphical models using a stochastic block model. Manuscript submitted for publication.

title: Mixed Markov Random Field
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
The mixed MRF is a graphical model for datasets containing both discrete (binary or ordinal) and continuous variables. bgms fits a mixed MRF automatically when variable_type includes both discrete and continuous types.

title: Mixed Markov Random Field
section: When to use a mixed MRF
text:
When to use a mixed MRF
Use a mixed MRF when the dataset contains a mix of variable types — for example, ordinal symptom ratings alongside continuous physiological measurements. Rather than discretizing continuous variables or treating ordinal scores as continuous, the mixed MRF models each variable according to its measurement scale.

title: Mixed Markov Random Field
text:
The model
The mixed MRF combines the ordinal MRF (for discrete variables) and the GGM (for continuous variables) into a single joint distribution. The model includes three types of pairwise interactions:

Discrete–discrete: interactions between ordinal/binary variables, as in the ordinal MRF.
Continuous–continuous: partial correlations between continuous variables, as in the GGM (encoded in a precision-like matrix \(K_{yy}\)).
Cross-type: interactions between discrete and continuous variables, capturing how a change in an ordinal variable’s category is associated with a shift in a continuous variable’s conditional mean.

title: Mixed Markov Random Field
text:
Data requirements
Each column in the data frame must have a corresponding entry in variable_type. Allowed types are "ordinal", "blume-capel", and "continuous". A per-variable vector is required when the types differ:
# Example: first 3 variables ordinal, last 2 continuous
fit = bgm(
  x = data,
  variable_type = c("ordinal", "ordinal", "ordinal",
                     "continuous", "continuous"),
  seed = 1234
)
bgms validates that ordinal variables contain integer-valued responses and that continuous variables are numeric. Missing values are handled by na_action ("listwise" or "impute"), just as for single-type models.

title: Mixed Markov Random Field
text:
Pseudolikelihood options
For mixed MRFs, the pseudolikelihood argument controls how the discrete full conditional distributions are approximated:

"conditional" (default): conditions on the observed continuous variables when computing the discrete full conditionals. This is faster because the discrete pseudolikelihood does not depend on the continuous interaction matrix \(K_{yy}\).
"marginal": integrates out the continuous variables, so the discrete full conditionals account for indirect associations induced through the continuous block. This is more expensive per iteration but may be more appropriate when discrete-continuous coupling is strong.

title: Mixed Markov Random Field
text:
Interpreting the output
The coef() method returns a single $pairwise matrix that contains all three types of interactions. The diagonal entries correspond to the \(K_{yy}\) diagonal (for continuous variables) or are zero (for discrete variables). The off-diagonal entries are pairwise interactions regardless of variable type.
The $indicator matrix (when edge selection is active) reports posterior inclusion probabilities for all edges, including cross-type edges.

title: Mixed Markov Random Field
text:
Fitting a mixed MRF
fit = bgm(
  x = data,
  variable_type = c("ordinal", "ordinal", "continuous", "continuous"),
  seed = 1234
)
summary(fit)
coef(fit)
The workflow — fitting, summarizing, extracting coefficients, checking diagnostics — is the same as for pure ordinal or pure continuous models.

title: MCMC Output
text:
The fit object
Both bgm() and bgmCompare() return a list (of class "bgms" or "bgmCompare") containing posterior summaries, posterior mean matrices, raw MCMC samples, and metadata.
fit = bgm(x = data, seed = 1234)

title: MCMC Output
text:
Posterior summaries
The summary() method prints formatted tables of posterior statistics. Each table includes:



Column
Meaning

Posterior mean


sd
Posterior standard deviation


MCSE
Monte Carlo standard error


n_eff

Rhat

For pairwise effects under edge selection, two additional columns appear:



Column
Meaning

Access specific summary tables with:
summary(fit)$pairwise   # pairwise interactions
summary(fit)$main        # category thresholds (ordinal) or means (GGM)
summary(fit)$indicator   # inclusion indicators (if edge selection active)

text:
Posterior mean matrices
The coef() method returns posterior means in matrix form:
coef(fit)$pairwise   # p x p symmetric matrix of interaction strengths
coef(fit)$indicator   # p x p symmetric matrix of inclusion probabilities
For ordinal models, coef(fit)$main returns a matrix of category threshold means (variables in rows, categories in columns). For mixed MRFs, it returns a list with $discrete and $continuous components.

title: MCMC Output
text:
Raw MCMC samples
For custom analyses, the raw posterior draws are stored in fit$raw_samples:
str(fit$raw_samples, max.level = 1)
The structure is:

$main: list of matrices (one per chain), each with rows = iterations and columns = main effect parameters.
$pairwise: list of matrices (one per chain) for pairwise interactions.
$indicator: list of matrices for edge indicators (if edge selection was active).
$allocations: list of matrices for cluster assignments (if SBM prior was used).
$nchains: number of chains.
$niter: number of post-warmup iterations per chain.
$parameter_names: named lists of parameter labels.

Each chain is stored separately, allowing per-chain diagnostics and trace plots (see MCMC Diagnostics).

title: Ordinal Markov Random Field
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
The ordinal Markov Random Field (MRF) is a graphical model for networks of binary and ordinal variables. It is the default model in bgms.

title: Ordinal Markov Random Field
text:
The model
For \(p\) ordinal variables with observations \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_p)\), the ordinal MRF specifies the joint distribution as:
\[
p(\mathbf{x}) \propto \exp\left(\sum_{i=1}^{p} \mu_{x_i}^{(i)} +
\sum_{i<j} \sigma_{ij} \, x_i \, x_j\right)
\]
where \(\mu_{x_i}^{(i)}\) are category threshold parameters for variable \(i\) (one per category above the lowest) and \(\sigma_{ij}\) is the pairwise interaction between variables \(i\) and \(j\).
A positive interaction \(\sigma_{ij} > 0\) means that higher categories of \(x_i\) tend to co-occur with higher categories of \(x_j\), conditional on all other variables. The category thresholds control the marginal distribution of each variable.

title: Ordinal Markov Random Field
text:
Regular ordinal variables
By default, bgms treats ordinal variables as “regular”: each category above the lowest receives its own threshold parameter. This imposes no constraint on the shape of the category distribution. Variables are internally recoded to consecutive integers starting at 0.
For binary variables (two categories, coded 0 and 1), the model reduces to the Ising model, a classical MRF for binary data. The single threshold parameter controls the probability of category 1 relative to category 0.

title: Ordinal Markov Random Field
text:
Blume-Capel variables
For ordinal variables with a natural baseline or reference category (e.g., a “neutral” response), the Blume-Capel parameterization models category thresholds as a quadratic function of distance from the baseline:
\[
\mu_c = \alpha \cdot (c - b) + \beta \cdot (c - b)^2
\]
where \(c\) is the category, \(b\) is the baseline category, \(\alpha\) captures the linear trend across categories, and \(\beta\) captures the preference toward or away from the baseline:

\(\beta < 0\): the model favors responses near the baseline category
\(\beta > 0\): the model favors extreme responses (far from the baseline)

Pairwise interactions between Blume-Capel variables use centered scores \((c - b)\) rather than raw category values.
To use Blume-Capel variables, set variable_type = "blume-capel" and provide the baseline_category argument:
fit = bgm(x = data, variable_type = "blume-capel",
          baseline_category = 2, seed = 1234)
The baseline_category can be a single integer (applied to all variables) or a vector of length \(p\).

title: Ordinal Markov Random Field
text:
Pseudolikelihood
The normalizing constant of the ordinal MRF is intractable for all but the smallest networks. bgms uses a pseudolikelihood approximation: the product of full conditional distributions replaces the joint distribution. This makes estimation feasible for networks with many variables while retaining consistent parameter estimates.

title: Ordinal Markov Random Field
text:
Fitting an ordinal MRF
The ordinal MRF is the default model type. For ordinal or binary data, call bgm() directly:
fit = bgm(x = data, seed = 1234)
For Blume-Capel variables specifically:
fit = bgm(x = data, variable_type = "blume-capel",
          baseline_category = 3, seed = 1234)
The output contains posterior summaries for both threshold parameters (posterior_summary_main) and pairwise interactions (posterior_summary_pairwise).

title: Ordinal Markov Random Field
text:
References
Marsman, M., van den Bergh, D., & Haslbeck, J. M. B. (2025). Bayesian analysis of the ordinal Markov random field. Psychometrika, 90(1), 146–182.

title: MCMC Diagnostics
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
Before interpreting results from bgm() or bgmCompare(), check that the MCMC sampler has converged and that posterior estimates are reliable. This chapter covers the diagnostic tools available in bgms.

title: MCMC Diagnostics
text:
Effective sample size (ESS)
The effective sample size estimates how many independent draws the MCMC chain is equivalent to. Correlated draws reduce the effective information per sample. A larger ESS means more precise posterior estimates.
The summary() output reports n_eff for each parameter. Values of n_eff above 400 are generally sufficient for reliable posterior means and credible intervals. Lower values suggest that more iterations may be needed.

Mixture ESS for edge-selected parameters
When edge selection is active, pairwise effects are governed by spike-and-slab priors. The parameter is set to exactly zero when the edge is excluded, creating a chain that mixes between zero and nonzero values.
Two ESS measures are reported:

n_eff: the unconditional ESS, computed from the full chain (including zeros). Measures how precisely the overall posterior mean is estimated.
n_eff_mixt: the mixture ESS, which accounts for additional uncertainty from the spike-and-slab switching. When the indicator rarely switches (fewer than 5 transitions), n_eff_mixt is suppressed.

title: MCMC Diagnostics
text:
R-hat
R-hat (split R-hat) compares the between-chain and within-chain variance. Values close to 1.0 indicate that the chains have converged to the same distribution. R-hat values above 1.01 suggest that the chains have not mixed and should be run longer.
bgms reports R-hat in summary() output and through extract_rhat().

title: MCMC Diagnostics
text:
Trace plots
Visually inspecting the sampled values across iterations is a direct way to assess convergence. Chains that have converged look like random noise fluctuating around a stable mean; chains that have not converged show trends, level shifts, or poor mixing.
Raw samples are accessible through fit$raw_samples:
param_index = 1
chains = fit$raw_samples$pairwise
nchains = length(chains)
cols = c("firebrick", "steelblue", "darkgreen", "goldenrod")

plot(chains[[1]][, param_index], type = "l", col = cols[1],
  xlab = "Iteration", ylab = "Value",
  main = "Traceplot",
  ylim = range(sapply(chains, function(ch) range(ch[, param_index]))))
if(nchains > 1) {
  for(c in 2:nchains) {
    lines(chains[[c]][, param_index], col = cols[c])
  }
}

title: MCMC Diagnostics
text:
NUTS-specific diagnostics
When using update_method = "nuts" (the default), additional diagnostics are stored in fit$nuts_diag.

E-BFMI
E-BFMI (Energy Bayesian Fraction of Missing Information) measures how efficiently the sampler explores the posterior. It compares the typical size of energy changes between successive samples to the overall spread of energies. Values close to 1 indicate efficient exploration; values below 0.3 suggest the sampler may be getting stuck.
A low E-BFMI does not necessarily mean the results are wrong, but it does warrant investigation. In models with edge selection, the most common cause is that the warmup period was too short for the discrete graph structure to equilibrate. Increasing warmup often resolves this.


Divergent transitions
Divergent transitions occur when the numerical integrator encounters regions where the posterior curvature changes too rapidly for the current step size. A small number of divergences (fewer than 0.1% of samples) is generally acceptable. Many divergences indicate that the sampler may be missing important parts of the posterior.
If divergences are frequent, increase target_accept (which reduces the step size). If that does not help, try update_method = "adaptive-metropolis" and compare results.


Tree depth
NUTS builds trajectories by repeatedly doubling their length until a U-turn criterion is satisfied. If the trajectory frequently reaches the maximum allowed depth (nuts_max_depth, default 10), the sampler may benefit from longer trajectories. Hitting the maximum depth occasionally is normal; hitting it on most iterations may indicate challenging posterior geometry. Consider increasing nuts_max_depth.

title: MCMC Diagnostics
text:
Warmup equilibration check
In models with edge selection, the discrete graph structure may take longer to reach stationarity than the continuous parameters. Even after warmup completes, the first portion of the sampling phase may still show transient behavior.
The fit$nuts_diag$warmup_check component provides diagnostics comparing the first and second halves of the post-warmup samples:







Field
Meaning




warmup_incomplete
TRUE if any indicator below suggests non-stationarity


energy_slope
Slope of energy vs. iteration; near zero = stable


slope_significant
TRUE if energy slope is significant (p < 0.01)


ebfmi_first_half
E-BFMI for the first half of post-warmup samples


ebfmi_second_half
E-BFMI for the second half


var_ratio
Ratio of energy variance (first half / second half); > 2 suggests settling



If these diagnostics suggest the chain was still settling, increase warmup and refit. If diagnostics remain problematic after doubling or tripling warmup, try refitting with update_method = "adaptive-metropolis" and compare posterior summaries. If the two samplers produce similar results, the estimates are likely trustworthy despite the warnings; if they differ, further investigation is warranted.

title: MCMC Diagnostics
text:
Recommended workflow

Inspect summary(): check R-hat (< 1.01) and ESS (> 400) for all parameters.
Check NUTS diagnostics: fit$nuts_diag$summary for divergences, tree depth saturation, and E-BFMI.
Check warmup: fit$nuts_diag$warmup_check for signs of incomplete equilibration.
Plot traces: visually inspect a few key parameters for mixing and stationarity.
If problems are found: increase warmup and/or iter, adjust target_accept, or switch samplers.

title: bgm
text:
Description
The bgm function estimates the pseudoposterior distribution of the parameters of a Markov Random Field (MRF) for binary, ordinal, continuous, or mixed (discrete and continuous) variables. Depending on the variable types, the model is an ordinal MRF, a Gaussian graphical model (GGM), or a mixed MRF. Optionally, it performs Bayesian edge selection using spike-and-slab priors to infer the network structure.

title: bgm
text:
Usage
bgm(
  x,
  variable_type = "ordinal",
  baseline_category,
  iter = 1000,
  warmup = 1000,
  pairwise_scale = 2.5,
  main_alpha = 0.5,
  main_beta = 0.5,
  edge_selection = TRUE,
  edge_prior = c("Bernoulli", "Beta-Bernoulli", "Stochastic-Block"),
  inclusion_probability = 0.5,
  beta_bernoulli_alpha = 1,
  beta_bernoulli_beta = 1,
  beta_bernoulli_alpha_between = 1,
  beta_bernoulli_beta_between = 1,
  dirichlet_alpha = 1,
  lambda = 1,
  na_action = c("listwise", "impute"),
  update_method = c("nuts", "adaptive-metropolis", "hamiltonian-mc"),
  target_accept,
  hmc_num_leapfrogs = 100,
  nuts_max_depth = 10,
  learn_mass_matrix = TRUE,
  chains = 4,
  cores = parallel::detectCores(),
  display_progress = c("per-chain", "total", "none"),
  seed = NULL,
  standardize = FALSE,
  pseudolikelihood = c("conditional", "marginal"),
  verbose = getOption("bgms.verbose", TRUE)
)

title: bgm
text:
Arguments

Data







Argument
Description




x
A data frame or matrix with n rows and p columns containing binary and ordinal responses. Variables are automatically recoded to non-negative integers (0, 1, ..., m). For regular ordinal variables, unobserved categories are collapsed; for Blume–Capel variables, all categories are retained.


variable_type
Character or character vector specifying the type of each variable. Allowed values: "ordinal", "blume-capel", or "continuous". A single string applies to all variables. A per-variable vector that mixes discrete ("ordinal" / "blume-capel") and "continuous" types fits a mixed MRF. Binary variables are automatically treated as "ordinal". Default: "ordinal".


baseline_category
Integer or vector. Baseline category for Blume–Capel variables. Can be a single integer (applied to all) or a vector of length p. Required if at least one variable is of type "blume-capel".


na_action
How to handle missing data: "listwise" (drop rows with missing values) or "impute" (single imputation during sampling). Default: "listwise".





Prior specification







Argument
Description




pairwise_scale
Scale of the Cauchy prior for pairwise interaction parameters. Default: 2.5.


main_alpha, main_beta
Shape parameters of the beta-prime prior for threshold parameters. Must be positive. Defaults: 0.5.


edge_selection
Logical. Whether to perform Bayesian edge selection. If FALSE, the model estimates all edges. Default: TRUE.


edge_prior
Prior for edge inclusion: "Bernoulli", "Beta-Bernoulli", or "Stochastic-Block". Default: "Bernoulli".


inclusion_probability
Prior inclusion probability of each edge (Bernoulli prior). Default: 0.5.


beta_bernoulli_alpha, beta_bernoulli_beta
Shape parameters for the beta distribution in the Beta–Bernoulli and Stochastic-Block priors. For the Stochastic-Block prior these are the within-cluster parameters. Defaults: 1.


beta_bernoulli_alpha_between, beta_bernoulli_beta_between
Shape parameters for between-cluster edge inclusion probabilities in the Stochastic-Block prior. Defaults: 1.


dirichlet_alpha
Concentration parameter of the Dirichlet prior on block assignments (Stochastic Block model). Default: 1.


lambda
Rate of the zero-truncated Poisson prior on the number of clusters (Stochastic Block model). Default: 1.


standardize
Logical. If TRUE, the Cauchy prior scale for each pairwise interaction is adjusted based on the range of response scores. Variables with more response categories have larger score products, so standardization ensures equivalent relative shrinkage across all pairs. Default: FALSE.





Sampler settings







Argument
Description




iter
Number of post-warmup iterations per chain. Default: 1000.


warmup
Number of warmup iterations before collecting samples. A minimum of 1000 is enforced. Default: 1000.


update_method
Sampling algorithm: "nuts" (No-U-Turn Sampler), "adaptive-metropolis" (componentwise Metropolis–Hastings with Robbins–Monro adaptation), or "hamiltonian-mc" (HMC with fixed path length). Default: "nuts".


target_accept
Target acceptance rate (0 to 1). Defaults: 0.44 for adaptive Metropolis, 0.65 for HMC, 0.80 for NUTS.


hmc_num_leapfrogs
Number of leapfrog steps for HMC. Default: 100.


nuts_max_depth
Maximum tree depth in NUTS. Default: 10.


learn_mass_matrix
Logical. If TRUE, adapt a diagonal mass matrix during warmup (HMC/NUTS only). Default: TRUE.


chains
Number of parallel chains. Default: 4.


cores
Number of CPU cores for parallel execution. Default: parallel::detectCores().


display_progress
Progress reporting: "per-chain", "total", or "none". Default: "per-chain".


seed
Optional integer seed for reproducibility.


pseudolikelihood
For mixed MRF models: "conditional" (conditions on continuous variables for discrete updates; faster) or "marginal" (integrates out continuous variables; more expensive). Ignored for pure ordinal or pure continuous data. Default: "conditional".


verbose
Logical. Print informational messages during data processing. Default: getOption("bgms.verbose", TRUE).

title: bgm
text:
Value
A list of class "bgms" with posterior summaries, posterior mean matrices, and access to raw MCMC draws. The object can be passed to print(), summary(), and coef().
Main components:

posterior_summary_main — Data frame with posterior summaries (mean, sd, MCSE, ESS, Rhat) for main-effect parameters. For OMRF models these are category thresholds; for mixed MRF models these are discrete thresholds and continuous means. NULL for GGM models.
posterior_summary_quadratic — Data frame with posterior summaries for the precision matrix diagonal (GGM and mixed MRF). NULL for OMRF models.
posterior_summary_pairwise — Data frame with posterior summaries for pairwise interaction parameters.
posterior_summary_indicator — Data frame with posterior summaries for edge inclusion indicators (if edge_selection = TRUE).
posterior_mean_main — Posterior mean of main-effect parameters.
posterior_mean_pairwise — Symmetric matrix of posterior mean pairwise interaction strengths. For GGM and mixed MRF models, the precision matrix diagonal is on the matrix diagonal.
posterior_mean_indicator — Symmetric matrix of posterior mean inclusion probabilities (if edge selection was enabled).
raw_samples — A list of raw MCMC draws per chain, with sublists for main, pairwise, indicator, and allocations (SBM prior).
arguments — A list of function call arguments and metadata.

Additional summaries when edge_prior = "Stochastic-Block":

posterior_summary_pairwise_allocations — Data frame with posterior summaries for pairwise cluster co-occurrence.
posterior_coclustering_matrix — Symmetric co-clustering proportion matrix.
posterior_mean_allocations — Posterior mean cluster allocations.
posterior_mode_allocations — Posterior mode cluster allocations.
posterior_num_blocks — Posterior probabilities for each possible number of clusters.

NUTS diagnostics (tree depth, divergences, energy, E-BFMI) are available in fit$nuts_diag when update_method = "nuts".

title: bgm
text:
Details

Ordinal variables
The function supports two types of ordinal variables.
Regular ordinal variables assign a category threshold parameter to each response category except the lowest. The model imposes no additional constraints on the distribution of category responses.
Blume–Capel ordinal variables assume a baseline category (e.g., a “neutral” response) and score responses by distance from this baseline. Category thresholds are modeled as:
\[\mu_c = \alpha \cdot (c - b) + \beta \cdot (c - b)^2\]
where \(\mu_c\) is the category threshold for category \(c\), \(\alpha\) is a linear trend across categories, \(\beta\) is a quadratic effect (negative values favor responses near the baseline; positive values favor extremes), and \(b\) is the baseline category.


Edge selection
When edge_selection = TRUE, the function performs Bayesian variable selection on pairwise interactions using spike-and-slab priors:

Bernoulli — Fixed inclusion probability across edges.
Beta-Bernoulli — Inclusion probability is given a Beta prior.
Stochastic-Block — Cluster-based edge priors with Beta, Dirichlet, and Poisson hyperpriors.



Prior distributions

Pairwise effects — Cauchy (slab) prior.
Main effects — Beta-prime distribution.
Edge indicators — Bernoulli, Beta-Bernoulli, or Stochastic-Block prior.



Sampling algorithms and warmup
Parameters are updated within a Gibbs framework using one of three algorithms:

Adaptive Metropolis–Hastings — Componentwise random-walk updates with Robbins–Monro proposal adaptation.
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo — Joint updates using fixed-length leapfrog trajectories. Step size is tuned during warmup via dual averaging; the diagonal mass matrix can also be adapted.
No-U-Turn Sampler — Adaptive extension of HMC with dynamically chosen trajectory lengths. Warmup uses a staged fast–slow–fast schedule.

When edge_selection = TRUE, edge-inclusion indicator updates are delayed until after the core warmup phase. The warmup schedule appends additional stages for proposal-SD tuning (Stage 3b) and graph initialization (Stage 3c), so the total warmup exceeds the user-specified value.


Missing data
If na_action = "listwise", rows with missing values are removed. If na_action = "impute", missing values are imputed within the MCMC loop via Gibbs sampling.

title: bgm
text:
Examples

# Fit a model on a subset of the Wenchuan data
fit = bgm(x = Wenchuan[, 1:5], chains = 2)

# Posterior inclusion probabilities
summary(fit)$indicator

# Posterior pairwise effects
summary(fit)$pairwise

title: bgmCompare
text:
Description
The bgmCompare function estimates group differences in category threshold parameters (main effects) and pairwise interactions (pairwise effects) of a Markov Random Field (MRF) for binary and ordinal variables. Groups can be defined either by supplying two separate datasets (x and y) or by a group membership vector. Optionally, Bayesian variable selection identifies differences across groups.

text:
Usage
bgmCompare(

  y,
  group_indicator,
  difference_selection = TRUE,
  main_difference_selection = FALSE,
  variable_type = "ordinal",
  baseline_category,
  difference_scale = 1,
  difference_prior = c("Bernoulli", "Beta-Bernoulli"),
  difference_probability = 0.5,
  beta_bernoulli_alpha = 1,
  beta_bernoulli_beta = 1,
  pairwise_scale = 2.5,
  main_alpha = 0.5,
  main_beta = 0.5,
  iter = 1000,
  warmup = 1000,
  na_action = c("listwise", "impute"),
  update_method = c("nuts", "adaptive-metropolis", "hamiltonian-mc"),
  target_accept,
  hmc_num_leapfrogs = 100,
  nuts_max_depth = 10,
  learn_mass_matrix = TRUE,
  chains = 4,
  cores = parallel::detectCores(),
  display_progress = c("per-chain", "total", "none"),
  seed = NULL,
  standardize = FALSE,
  verbose = getOption("bgms.verbose", TRUE)
)

title: bgmCompare
text:
Arguments

Data and groups







Argument
Description




x
A data frame or matrix of binary and ordinal responses for Group 1. Variables should be coded as nonnegative integers starting at 0. For ordinal variables, unused categories are collapsed; for Blume–Capel variables, all categories are retained.


y
Optional data frame or matrix for Group 2 (two-group designs). Must have the same variables (columns) as x.


group_indicator
Optional integer vector of group memberships for rows of x (multi-group designs). Ignored if y is supplied.


variable_type
Character vector specifying the type of each variable: "ordinal" (default) or "blume-capel".


baseline_category
Integer or vector giving the baseline category for Blume–Capel variables.


na_action
How to handle missing data: "listwise" (drop rows) or "impute" (impute within Gibbs). Default: "listwise".





Difference selection







Argument
Description




difference_selection
Logical. If TRUE, spike-and-slab priors are applied to difference parameters. Default: TRUE.


main_difference_selection
Logical. If TRUE, apply spike-and-slab selection to main effect (threshold) differences. Since main effects are often nuisance parameters and their selection can interfere with pairwise selection under the Beta-Bernoulli prior, the default is FALSE. Only used when difference_selection = TRUE.


difference_scale
Scale of the Cauchy prior for difference parameters. Default: 1.


difference_prior
Prior for difference inclusion: "Bernoulli" or "Beta-Bernoulli". Default: "Bernoulli".


difference_probability
Prior inclusion probability for differences (Bernoulli prior). Default: 0.5.


beta_bernoulli_alpha, beta_bernoulli_beta
Shape parameters of the Beta prior for inclusion probabilities in the Beta–Bernoulli model. Defaults: 1.





Prior specification







Argument
Description




pairwise_scale
Scale of the Cauchy prior for baseline pairwise interactions. Default: 2.5.


main_alpha, main_beta
Shape parameters of the beta-prime prior for baseline threshold parameters. Defaults: 0.5.


standardize
Logical. If TRUE, the Cauchy prior scale for each pairwise interaction (both baseline and difference) is adjusted based on the range of response scores. Default: FALSE.





Sampler settings







Argument
Description




iter
Number of post-warmup iterations per chain. Default: 1000.


warmup
Number of warmup iterations before sampling. Default: 1000.


update_method
Sampling algorithm: "nuts", "adaptive-metropolis", or "hamiltonian-mc". Default: "nuts".


target_accept
Target acceptance rate. Defaults: 0.44 (Metropolis), 0.65 (HMC), 0.80 (NUTS).


hmc_num_leapfrogs
Leapfrog steps for HMC. Default: 100.


nuts_max_depth
Maximum tree depth for NUTS. Default: 10.


learn_mass_matrix
Logical. If TRUE, adapts a diagonal mass matrix during warmup (HMC/NUTS only). Default: TRUE.


chains
Number of parallel chains. Default: 4.


cores
Number of CPU cores. Default: parallel::detectCores().


display_progress
Progress reporting: "per-chain", "total", or "none". Default: "per-chain".


seed
Optional integer seed for reproducibility.


verbose
Logical. Print informational messages during data processing. Default: getOption("bgms.verbose", TRUE).

title: bgmCompare
text:
Value
A list of class "bgmCompare" containing posterior summaries, posterior mean matrices, and raw MCMC samples:

posterior_summary_main_baseline, posterior_summary_pairwise_baseline — Summaries of baseline thresholds and pairwise interactions.
posterior_summary_main_differences, posterior_summary_pairwise_differences — Summaries of group differences in thresholds and pairwise interactions.
posterior_summary_indicator — Summaries of inclusion indicators (if difference_selection = TRUE).
posterior_mean_main_baseline, posterior_mean_pairwise_baseline — Posterior mean matrices (legacy style).
raw_samples — List of raw draws per chain for main, pairwise, and indicator parameters.
arguments — List of function call arguments and metadata.

The summary() method prints formatted summaries, and coef() extracts posterior means. NUTS diagnostics are available in fit$nuts_diag when update_method = "nuts".

title: bgmCompare
text:
Details

Pairwise interactions
For variables \(i\) and \(j\), the group-specific interaction is represented as:
\[\theta_{ij}^{(g)} = \phi_{ij} + \delta_{ij}^{(g)}\]
where \(\phi_{ij}\) is the baseline effect and \(\delta_{ij}^{(g)}\) are group differences constrained to sum to zero.


Ordinal variables
Regular ordinal variables: category thresholds are decomposed into a baseline plus group differences for each category.
Blume–Capel variables: category thresholds are quadratic in the category index, with both the linear and quadratic terms split into a baseline plus group differences.


Variable selection
When difference_selection = TRUE, spike-and-slab priors are applied to difference parameters:

Bernoulli — Fixed prior inclusion probability.
Beta-Bernoulli — Inclusion probability given a Beta prior.



Sampling algorithms and warmup
Parameters are updated within a Gibbs framework, using the same sampling algorithms and staged warmup scheme described in bgm(): adaptive Metropolis–Hastings, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, or the No-U-Turn Sampler. When difference_selection = TRUE, indicator updates are delayed until late warmup.

title: bgmCompare
text:
Examples

# Compare French and non-French groups on a subset of the Boredom data
x = Boredom[Boredom$language == "fr", 2:6]
y = Boredom[Boredom$language != "fr", 2:6]

fit = bgmCompare(x, y, chains = 2)

# Posterior inclusion probabilities
summary(fit)$indicator

# Bayesian model averaged main effects for the groups
coef(fit)$main_effects_groups

# Bayesian model averaged pairwise effects for the groups
coef(fit)$pairwise_effects_groups
